title: Nothing
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 29 of 40
content:
Danse’s grief arrived late.

At first there had been tasks.

Avoid Brotherhood patrols. Secure Bravo. Find food. Repair equipment. Trade with settlements. Learn how to exist without a rank.

Then the tasks became routine.

That was when the bottom fell out.

I woke one morning and found him sitting at the table staring at his old Brotherhood undersuit folded in front of him.

He had been there long enough for the coffee to go cold.

“Danse?”

No response.

I sat across from him.

His eyes looked through me.

“What’s happening?”

He swallowed.

“I don’t know.”

“Do you want me here?”

A pause.

“Yes.”

So I stayed.

Hours passed.

He spoke in pieces.

Everything I had.

Everything I knew.

Gone.

He had built his entire life around a plan: join, serve, rise, protect, die usefully someday. Even fear had fit inside it.

Now there was no plan large enough to contain him.

“I started out as nothing,” he said, “and somehow I ended up there again.”

I hated the sentence.

Not him.

The cruelty of it.

“You are not nothing.”

“You can’t know that.”

“I can.”

“How?”

“Because nothing doesn’t make coffee badly on purpose.”

He looked at me.

“I don’t make it badly on purpose.”

“Debatable.”

A tiny shift in his face.

I kept going.

“Nothing doesn’t remember Brach’s cards or Worwick’s snoring. Nothing doesn’t carry RadAway for a ghoul after insulting him. Nothing doesn’t argue with me about weapon stocks for forty minutes.”

“That was thirty.”

“See?”

His mouth trembled.

Then he began to cry.

Quietly at first.

Danse seemed furious about it.

He turned away.

I moved around the table and knelt beside him.

“Don’t look at me.”

“No.”

“I mean it.”

“So do I.”

His hands clenched.

“This is pathetic.”

“No.”

“I spent years telling soldiers to control themselves.”

“You spent years telling soldiers not to panic in combat. This is not combat.”

“It feels worse.”

“I know.”

That undid him.

He bent forward, elbows on his knees, both hands covering his face.

I held him.

There was nothing graceful about it.

His shoulders shook. My knees hurt against the bunker floor. At some point I started crying too, which annoyed me because I was trying to be useful.

Eventually the storm inside him weakened.

Danse leaned back against the chair.

“I’m sorry.”

“No.”

“I got your shirt wet.”

“That is an acceptable operational loss.”

He laughed weakly.

I sat on the floor beside him.

After a while he said, “What if none of my past happened?”

“Some of it did.”

“You don’t know where the line is.”

“No.”

“Cutler could be invented.”

“Yes.”

The word hurt him.

I kept going because lying would hurt more later.

“But your grief is real.”

He looked at me.

“If someone built the memory, they built the wound too. You’ve lived with it. It shaped choices you actually made.”

“That doesn’t make Cutler real.”

“No.”

He closed his eyes.

“What do I do with that?”

“Whatever you need.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the only one I have.”

We sat in silence.

Then Danse reached for the folded Brotherhood uniform.

He did not put it on.

He unfolded it and ran his fingers over the insignia.

“I loved them.”

“I know.”

“I still do.”

“I know.”

“They wanted me dead.”

“Yes.”

He looked ashamed of the contradiction.

I touched his hand.

“People can hurt you and still matter. Institutions too.”

“That seems inefficient.”

“Emotion usually is.”

He breathed out.

“Terrible system.”

“Court-martial the designer.”

That got a real laugh.

Small.

But real.

That night he put the uniform in a storage trunk.

Not burned.

Not displayed.

Stored.

Another thing he was not ready to decide.

Before sleep, Danse lay beside me in the dark.

“Are you still here?” he asked.

The question was so quiet it hurt.

I turned toward him.

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to be.”

He stared at me.

No rank. No purpose. No tactical advantage.

Want.

Danse touched my face.

“Thank you.”

I kissed his palm.

He closed his eyes.

For that night, being wanted was enough.

Grief did not leave after that morning.

It changed shifts.

Some days Danse woke functional enough to repair a rifle before breakfast and spend six hours helping a settlement reinforce a wall.

Other days one sound could dismantle him.

A vertibird passed over Bravo three weeks after Maxson spared him.

Danse was outside chopping firewood.

The axe stopped mid-swing.

I watched his face turn toward the sky.

The aircraft was too high to see markings clearly, but the engine note was Brotherhood.

Danse stood frozen until it disappeared.

Then he set the axe down with exquisite care.

“I’m going inside.”

“All right.”

He walked past me without looking up.

I gave him ten minutes before following.

He sat on the edge of the bed holding the detective novel closed in both hands.

“You want company?”

“I don’t know.”

“Can I sit?”

A pause.

“Yes.”

I sat on the floor instead of the bed, close enough to be available without trapping him.

Danse stared at the bunker wall.

“I knew the pilot.”

“The one who flew over?”

“I couldn’t see. I just…”

He rubbed his thumb along the book cover.

“Every vertibird sounds like someone I knew.”

I nodded.

He swallowed.

“I keep thinking I should send Haylen a message.”

“Do you want to?”

“Yes.”

“Then why don’t you?”

“Because contact could put her in danger.”

“That sounds real.”

“And because if she doesn’t answer…”

His voice stopped.

There was the other fear.

Not tactical.

Rejection.

I moved onto the bed beside him.

“What would you say?”

Danse gave me a suspicious look.

“I’m not suggesting you send it. Just say it here.”

He looked down.

At first I thought he would refuse.

Then he began.

“Haylen. I hope you’re safe.”

The formal tone made my chest ache.

“I hope Rhys hasn’t gotten himself killed through stubbornness.”

“Likely impossible.”

A faint smile.

Danse continued.

“I’m sorry I left without explaining. At the time I believed…”

He stopped.

“What?”

“That I would be dead before an explanation mattered.”

The room became very quiet.

I put my hand over his.

He went on.

“I want you to know none of what happened changes what your service meant to me.”

His voice roughened.

“You were a good scribe. A better friend. I should have said that more often.”

His fingers tightened around mine.

“And I hope you never think my… nature makes your trust foolish.”

I hated that word in his mouth.

Nature.

As if being built had become a moral diagnosis.

“What would you want her to say back?” I asked.

Danse stared ahead.

“That she doesn’t regret knowing me.”

I waited.

“And?”

“That she’s angry.”

I blinked.

“Why?”

“Because Haylen gets angry when she’s frightened.”

The fondness in his voice was immediate.

“And because if she is angry, she is still…”

“Still your Haylen?”

His eyes closed.

“Yes.”

We did not send the message that day.

But we wrote it down.

That mattered.

The worst days were the ones with no obvious trigger.

Danse would wake, dress, check the perimeter, and then simply stop. Not dramatic. No collapse. He would sit with a wrench in his hand and stare at a bolt without turning it.

I learned not to fill every silence.

Sometimes I sat nearby and repaired my own gear.

Sometimes I read aloud from the terrible detective novel until he corrected the investigator’s procedure.

Once I made coffee so bad even Danse objected.

“That is undrinkable.”

“I used your method.”

“You did not.”

“I eyeballed everything and hoped discipline would compensate.”

“That is not my method.”

He took the pot away from me.

The argument lasted ten minutes.

It was the most alive he had looked all morning.

Grief did not always need to be defeated. Sometimes it needed enough company that it could not convince him nothing else existed.

At dinner, Danse ate two bowls of stew instead of one.

Afterward he finished another chapter of the detective novel and complained that the investigator had ignored obvious evidence.

“You’re enjoying it,” I said.

“The protagonist is incompetent.”

“You’re on page one hundred and six.”

“I need to see how bad it gets.”

“Obviously.”

He looked almost offended.

Then the corner of his mouth moved.

Before bed, Danse unfolded Haylen’s unsent letter again.

He did not add anything.

He simply read the words already there, folded the page, and placed it beside the detective novel.

“You don’t have to send it to make it real,” I said.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He looked at the paper.

“More than yesterday.”

That was enough movement for one day.

The lamp burned low. Danse turned another page, frowned at the detective’s reasoning, and kept reading anyway.

That, too, felt like a kind of survival.

Grief sat with us at the table.

So did appetite.

So did irritation.

So did love.

None cancelled the others.

That was becoming one of the hardest lessons Danse had ever learned.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
